text: This is an illustrative, fictional scenario built on Solari Vision Labs, written to make Chapter 6's FinOps warnings concrete instead of abstract -- not a report of any real company or incident. An ML engineer kicks off a routine fine-tuning run on a Friday afternoon, requesting four GPUs for an expected six-to-eight-hour job, and goes home for the weekend.

The training script does finish, late Friday night, and saves its final checkpoint successfully. But a background thread it launched earlier, for asynchronously uploading training-curve images, is not a daemon thread -- it never exits on its own. The main training loop returns, but the process itself keeps running, so Kubernetes never marks the Job Completed. Four GPUs stay held, status Running, all weekend and into the next week.

Two separate monitoring gaps let this go unnoticed for days. Nothing checked whether the Job had been Running far longer than a job like this normally takes. And nothing watched real GPU utilization on that node, which had dropped to roughly one or two percent the moment training actually stopped -- the earliest, most direct signal that something had stalled, well before any dollar figure would show up on a bill.

What finally surfaced it was a Thursday cloud-bill review, four days after the job should have finished -- four A100 GPUs held idle at the premium rate Chapter 6 described, for roughly four extra days. One stuck thread, not a fleet-wide problem, did the damage, and it compounded exactly the way that chapter warned a GPU mistake would.

Two Prometheus alert rules would have caught this far earlier. One fires when a training Job has been Running longer than its expected duration, regardless of why. The other fires when GPU utilization on a training node stays under five percent for thirty minutes straight, regardless of what Kubernetes' own status says. Either one alone would have caught it within an hour instead of four days -- which is exactly why a real practice needs both, not one or the other.

This case study is the concrete version of an abstract warning: GPU cost velocity leaves far less room for delay than a general cloud-cost review does. Lesson 32 closes the course by tracing every decision across this whole eight-chapter arc, from GPU fundamentals through this capstone, back to the chapter that made it possible.
